name: Giiwo
world_status: statement found in an open source

earlier_scan.source_named: Schuh, Russell G. 1978. Bole-Tangale languages of the Bauchi area (Northern Nigeria); Zoch, Ulrike 2014. Verbalmorphologie der Bole-Tangale-Sprachen

new_statements.quote: These languages all have two phonemic tones only. An occasional fall, analyzable as high-low on one syllable, is indicated. Rising tones are also found, but all examples here are on word final long vowels. In these cases it is difficult to determine whether this is Cĭi (a single syllable with a rising tone) or Cìyí (two syllables with the last syllable beginning in a semi-vowel homorganic to the vowels). A downstep (lowered high after high) is also found. In no case was downstep found to play an important morpho-syntactic role. It nearly always was an obvious contraction of high-low-high to high-downstep.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Giiwo (Kirfi) is described as a two-tone language (H, L; HL fall on one syllable; downstep from H-L-H contraction); every word in the Kirfi word list and paradigms is tone-marked. Schuh makes no statement about word stress or accent anywhere in the book, so no stress rule can be read off; the only prosodic property of record is lexical/grammatical tone (verb tone classes: monosyllabic and CVC- verbs high, CVVC-/CVCC- verbs low, p. 36).
new_statements.exceptions: None regarding stress (none stated). For tone: rising tones occur only on word-final long vowels; downstep is not morpho-syntactically important.
new_statements.domain_note: The tone statement is made in the general introduction for all five languages of the book (Bele, Kirfi, Galambu, Gera, Geruma), based on a four-to-six-hour elicitation session with Kirfi speakers at Kirfin Sama on 14 April 1975 (p. 32); word-level citation forms in a ~250-item word list plus perfective verb paradigms. Schuh states (p. 7) that 'detailed phonological descriptions' are missing from the sketches, so the absence of a stress statement is an absence of description, not an explicit denial of stress.
new_statements.identity_note: Schuh 1978 calls the language 'Kirfi' (abbrev. Ki); the book itself records the endonym bu giiwó 'Kirfi language', ba giiwó 'Kirfi person' (p. 32), so Kirfi = Giiwo [kks] giiw1236. Data are from Kirfin Sama (the Kirfi headquarters village) and speakers Sambo Kirfi and others, April 1975; Schuh notes 'apparently some dialect differences in Ki but no specifics were discovered' (p. 32). The tone statement quoted is a group-level statement covering Bele, Kirfi, Galambu, Gera and Geruma.

sources.note: Nothing on stress or accent anywhere (grep of scanned text for stress/accent/prominence/pitch: no hits; pages checked visually). Introduction 'Tones' p. 9: all five languages (Bele, Kirfi, Galambu, Gera, Geruma) have two phonemic tones only, with occasional HL fall, rising tones on word-final long vowels, and downstep as a contraction of H-L-H. Kirfi 'Remarks on Phonology' p. 33 covers only geminates and intervocalic y; Kirfi §7.1.2 p. 36 gives lexical tone classes of verbs. Author states p. 7 that detailed phonological descriptions are missing from the sketches. Word list fully tone-marked.
